## Proposition 10.33
**Statement:** To find two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them rational but the rectangle contained by them medial.

**Step 1.** By 10.30, find two rational straight lines AB, BC commensurable in square only such that the square on AB is greater than the square on BC by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AB.

**Step 2.** Bisect BC at D by 1.10. Then BD equals half of BC, so the square on BD is one-fourth of the square on BC.

**Step 3.** By 6.28, apply to AB a rectangle equal to the square on BD and deficient by a square figure. Let this rectangle be AE times EB, where E is a point on AB such that AE times EB equals the square on BD.

**Step 4.** Since the square on AB is greater than the square on BC by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AB (by construction in Step 1), and the rectangle AE times EB equals the square on BD which equals one-fourth of the square on BC, it follows by 10.18 that AE and EB are incommensurable in length.

**Step 5.** Describe a semicircle AGB on AB as diameter, using P3. From E, erect a perpendicular EG to AB meeting the semicircle at G, using 1.11. Join AG and GB by P1.

**Step 6.** Since AGB is a semicircle on diameter AB and G lies on the semicircle, the angle AGB is a right angle by 3.31.

**Step 7.** Since angle AGB is right and GE is perpendicular to AB, by 6.8 the triangles AGE, GBE are similar both to the whole triangle AGB and to one another.

**Step 8.** From the similarity of triangle AGE to triangle AGB (Step 7), we have AB is to AG as AG is to AE. By 6.17, the square on AG equals the rectangle AB times AE. Similarly, from the similarity of triangle GBE to triangle AGB, AB is to GB as GB is to EB, and by 6.17 the square on GB equals the rectangle AB times EB.

**Step 9.** Therefore the sum of the squares on AG and GB equals the rectangle AB times AE plus the rectangle AB times EB. By 2.1, this equals the rectangle AB times the whole line AB (since AE plus EB equals AB), which is the square on AB.

**Step 10.** Since AB is rational, the square on AB is rational by D10.1.4. Hence the sum of the squares on AG and GB is rational.

**Step 11.** From the similarity established in Step 7, in particular from triangle AGE being similar to triangle GBE, we have AE is to GE as GE is to EB. By 6.17, the square on GE equals the rectangle AE times EB, which by construction equals the square on BD.

**Step 12.** Since the square on GE equals the square on BD, and BD equals half of BC (Step 2), the square on GE is to the square on BC as one is to four, which is a ratio of square numbers. By 10.9, GE is commensurable in length with BC.

**Step 13.** Since BC is rational and GE is commensurable in length with BC (Step 12), GE is rational by D10.1.3.

**Step 14.** Since AB and BC are commensurable in square only, and GE is commensurable in length with BC (Step 12), if AB were commensurable in length with GE, then by 10.12 AB would be commensurable in length with BC, which contradicts the hypothesis. Hence AB is incommensurable in length with GE.

**Step 15.** Since GE is commensurable in length with BC, the square on GE is commensurable with the square on BC. Since AB and BC are commensurable in square, the square on AB is commensurable with the square on BC. By 10.12 applied to areas, the square on AB is commensurable with the square on GE. Hence AB and GE are commensurable in square.

**Step 16.** Therefore AB and GE are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. By 10.21, the rectangle contained by AB and GE is irrational, and it is medial.

**Step 17.** From the similarity in Step 7, triangle AGE is similar to triangle AGB, so AG is to GE as AB is to GB. By 6.16, the rectangle AG times GB equals the rectangle GE times AB.

**Step 18.** Since the rectangle GE times AB is medial (Step 16), the rectangle AG times GB, being equal to it (Step 17), is also medial.

**Step 19.** Since the square on AG equals AB times AE and the square on GB equals AB times EB (Step 8), the ratio of the square on AG to the square on GB equals the ratio AE to EB by 6.1. Since AE and EB are incommensurable in length (Step 4), they do not have to one another the ratio of a number to a number by 10.7. Hence the square on AG does not have to the square on GB the ratio of a number to a number. By 10.8, the squares on AG and GB are incommensurable, so AG and GB are incommensurable in square by D10.1.2.

**Step 20.** Therefore AG and GB are two straight lines incommensurable in square (Step 19) such that the sum of the squares on them is rational (Step 10) and the rectangle contained by them is medial (Step 18), which is what was required to find.

heath_proof_text: Let there be set out two rational straight lines AB, BC commensurable in square only and such that the square on the greater AB is greater than the square on the less BC by the square on a straight line incommensurable with AB, [X. 30] let BC be bisected at D, let there be applied to AB a parallelogram equal to the square on either of the straight lines BD, DC and deficient by a square figure, and let it be the rectangle AE, EB; [VI. 28] let the semicircle AFB be described on AB, let EF be drawn at right angles to AB, and let AF, FB be joined. Then, since AB, BC are unequal straight lines, and the square on AB is greater than the square on BC by the square on a straight line incommensurable with AB, while there has been applied to AB a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on BC, that is, to the square on half of it, and deficient by a square figure, making the rectangle AE, EB, therefore AE is incommensurable with EB. [X. 18] And, as AE is to EB, so is the rectangle BA, AE to the rectangle AB, BE, while the rectangle BA, AE is equal to the square on AF, and the rectangle AB, BE to the square on BF; therefore the square on AF is incommensurable with the square on FB; therefore AF, FB are incommensurable in square. And, since AB is rational, therefore the square on AB is also rational; so that the sum of the squares on AF, FB is also rational. [I. 47] And since, again, the rectangle AE, EB is equal to the square on EF, and, by hypothesis, the rectangle AE, EB is also equal to the square on BD, therefore FE is equal to BD; therefore BC is double of FE, so that the rectangle AB, BC is also commensurable with the rectangle AB, EF. But the rectangle AB, BC is medial; [X. 21] therefore the rectangle AB, EF is also medial. [X. 23] But the rectangle AB, EF is equal to the rectangle AF, FB; [Lemma]therefore the rectangle AF, FB is also medial. But it was also proved that the sum of the squares on these straight lines is rational. Therefore two straight lines AF, FB incommensurable in square have been found which make the sum of the squares on them rational, but the rectangle contained by them medial.
